lessons.title: Welcome to the club
lessons.html:
You joined because you have meant it before. New Year's, a Sunday morning, the car after an argument. You meant it every time, and it did not hold.

This club exists to fix that. Not with more conviction, but with a system: a mechanism, not a mood. Everything in here is built to show up on an ordinary Tuesday, in a way the people in your house could see without you announcing it.

What your membership includes

Here is what comes with your membership. Steps 1 to 7 and Month 1 are open today. Pay yearly and everything is open today.

  • The 7-step framework. Every worksheet from Step 1 to Step 7, in order, one lesson per step. This is the spine of the club.
  • Your monthly tools. All 11 tools from the store, a new set every 30 days until you have them all by month six: the Weekly Scorecard and Forty Cards first, then the marriage, fatherhood and faith tools.
  • The monthly tool. A new Club-only tool each month that is not sold anywhere else. It shows up in your members area when it is released.
  • The Thursday email. One email a week: a time, a trigger, and a way to tell if it held.
  • The monthly call and your partner. One live hour on Google Meet on the second Tuesday of every month, and if you want one, an accountability partner to trade Scorecards with every Sunday.

How to use the members area

Do not try to read everything this week. Men who binge every tool feel productive for two days and then stall. The order that works:

  1. Read the next lesson, "Your first week in the club". It gives you exactly three things to do in the next seven days.
  2. Work the framework one step at a time. Each step builds on the one before it. Step 1 ends in a one-sentence statement of the man you want to be, and every step after it gets checked against that sentence.
  3. Use each month's tools when they open, one set at a time. A tool you picked for a reason gets used. A tool you downloaded because it was free sits in a folder.
  4. Come back every Sunday. Your weekly review is where the system either holds or gets fixed.

Downloading your files

Every lesson that comes with a file has a download link in it. PDFs are made to be printed and written on with a pen, not filled in on your phone. The trackers are Excel files: open them in Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers and save your own copy.

The files are yours to keep. If you ever cancel, save them first; access to the members area ends when your membership does.

Before you move on: write down one line: the one area of your life where you most want this to hold (your marriage, your kids, your faith, or your discipline). It is the first thing you will check yourself against. If you want, reply to any Club email with it. It reaches Brian.

lessons.title: Your first week in the club
lessons.html:
Your first seven days have one job: to put a system in place before the enthusiasm wears off. Three things, in this order. None of them takes more than thirty minutes.

Day 1 or 2: do Step 1

Open Step 1: What type of man do you want to be? in the framework section. Print it. Sit somewhere without your phone, with a pen, for twenty minutes.

You will list the attributes of that man, write what each one looks like on an ordinary Tuesday, and describe how the people in your house would know without you telling them. It ends in one sentence that says who he is.

If you have already done Step 1 from the free download, do it again anyway. A second pass, a few weeks later, is almost always sharper than the first.

Day 3 or 4: set up the Weekly Scorecard

Go to Month 1: the Weekly Scorecard and Forty Cards under Your monthly tools and download it. Pick the decisions for your first week from your Step 1 sentence, and for each one write down three things before the week starts:

  • When it happens. "This week" is not a time. "Tuesday and Thursday, 9 pm, after the kids are down" is.
  • What counts as a miss. Decide it now, so a bad week is defined before, not argued about after.
  • How you would know it held. Could your wife see it without you announcing it? If not, it did not hold.

Then log it on the day it happens. Sunday-night memory is a story, not evidence.

Day 7: your first Sunday review

Block fifteen minutes on Sunday. Put your Step 1 sentence next to your scorecard and answer three questions honestly:

  1. Which decisions held, and which did not?
  2. For each miss, what was the trigger? A time that was never realistic, a situation you did not plan for, or simply no decision at all?
  3. What is the one change you will make to next week's scorecard?

Missing once is not failure. The sheet tells you exactly what is: a miss you never name.

Check yourself at the end of the week

  • You have a one-sentence statement of the man you want to be
  • Your scorecard has a when, a miss and a test for every decision
  • You logged each day on the day, not from memory
  • You named at least one miss and one change for next week

Then move to Step 2 and keep one step per week from here on. Say your Step 1 sentence out loud to one other man this week. Men who say it in front of other men tend to keep it.

lessons.title: The 6-minute training: you meant it every time
lessons.html:
▶ Watch the training on YouTube (5:50)

If you only have six minutes today, spend them here. The video is the whole Club in one sitting: why good men keep breaking the same promise, and why the fix is not more conviction but a system that shows up on an ordinary Tuesday.

Watch it once now, and again the night before your first Sunday review. It lands differently the second time, after you have tried to keep a decision for a week.

What to listen for

  • The three places promises die: no when, no defined miss, graded from memory
  • The wife test: would she notice without being told?
  • Why Step 1 comes before any goal
  • The four moves that turn the Step 1 question into one sentence

Where to go next

The video ends with an assignment for tonight. Everything you need for it is already here: open Step 1: what type of man do you want to be? in the framework section and download the worksheet. Then follow the plan in Your first week in the club for your scorecard and first Sunday review.

lessons.title: Step 1: what type of man do you want to be?
lessons.html:
Download the Step 1 worksheet (PDF)

Most men start with a goal: lose the weight, fix the temper, pray every morning. The goal feels like progress, but it has nothing underneath it. When the week gets hard, there is no reason to keep going that is bigger than the goal itself.

Step 1 comes before the goal. It asks one question, and the answer becomes the standard every later step is measured against.

How to work this step

Print the worksheet. Give it twenty minutes with a pen, not your phone. Work through it in this order:

  1. Name the attributes. Write down the qualities of the man you want to be. Patient. Present. Faithful. Steady under pressure. Use your own words.
  2. Make each one ordinary. For every attribute, write what it looks like on an ordinary Tuesday. "Patient" becomes "I do not raise my voice when homework runs late."
  3. Apply the house test. Write how the people you live with would know, without you telling them.
  4. Write the sentence. Finish with one sentence that says who he is.

What a finished sentence looks like

Here is an example of the kind of sentence this step is aiming for: "I am a man who is home when he is home, keeps his word to his wife, and lets his kids see him pray." Each part can be checked on a given day, and each part would be visible to someone else.

Compare it with "I want to be a better husband and father." That is true, but nobody could tell on Tuesday whether it held.

Before you move to Step 2

  • Every attribute has an ordinary-Tuesday version
  • Someone in your house could notice each one without being told
  • Your sentence fits on one line and you could say it from memory
  • You have written it somewhere you will see it every Sunday

Bring your sentence to the next monthly call, or send it to your accountability partner. Hearing how other men answered the same question is one of the fastest ways to sharpen your own.

lessons.title: Step 2: what are your goals?
lessons.html:
Download the Step 2 worksheet (PDF)

Now that you know who you want to be, you can decide what you are going after. The order matters. A goal set before Step 1 is chosen by mood: whatever felt urgent that week. A goal set after Step 1 is chosen because the man in your sentence would pursue it.

Use your Step 1 sentence as the filter

Keep your Step 1 sentence in front of you while you work the worksheet. For every goal you write down, ask one question: does this move me toward the man in that sentence, or is it just something I feel I should want?

Say your sentence includes "home when he is home". A goal to be off the phone from 6 to 8 pm on weeknights passes the filter. A goal to read fifty books this year might be good, but unless it connects to the sentence, it does not belong on this page yet.

Common mistakes at this step

  • Writing ten goals when three would actually get done
  • Keeping goals so vague you could never tell if you missed one
  • Copying someone else's goals instead of deriving them from your sentence
  • Adding a goal with no idea when in the week it would happen

The last mistake is the one Steps 3 to 6 are built to fix. A goal says what. A system says when. For now, just get the right goals on paper, and fewer of them than you think.

Before Step 3: you should be able to point at each goal and say which part of your Step 1 sentence it serves.

lessons.title: Step 3: what has stopped you so far?
lessons.html:
Download the Step 3 worksheet (PDF)

You have had goals like these before. Some of them you have set more than once. This step is an honest look at why they did not hold, so the system you build next is designed around the real reasons, not the ones you tell yourself.

Look for the pattern, not the excuse

An excuse explains one bad week: "work was crazy", "the kids were sick". A pattern explains why the same thing happens every time. When you work the worksheet, go back to specific attempts and look for what they had in common.

For example, a man who has tried three times to start praying in the morning might notice that every attempt died the first week he stayed up past midnight. The obstacle was never prayer. It was that his evenings had no end time. That is something a system can fix.

Questions to push past the first answer

  • When exactly did the last attempt stop, and what was happening that day?
  • Did the goal ever have a set time, or only good intentions?
  • Who knew about it, and did anyone notice when it stopped?
  • What did you tell yourself the first time you missed?

Be specific and be fair. The point is not to feel guilty. Guilt is a mood, and moods do not build anything. The point is to have a clear list of what the system needs to survive.

Before Step 4: you should have at least one obstacle written down that you have never said out loud before. If you are willing, name it on the next monthly call. You will not be the only one.

lessons.title: Step 4: the laws of a system that holds
lessons.html:
Download the Step 4 worksheet (PDF)

Steps 1 to 3 gave you three things: who you want to be, what you are going after, and what has stopped you before. This step is where they meet. A system that holds is one that was built with your obstacles in mind, not one that assumes you will feel motivated every day.

Test each law against your Step 3 list

As you read each law in the worksheet, put your Step 3 obstacles next to it. For every obstacle, find the law that would have caught it. If an obstacle is not covered by any law you are applying, your system has a gap, and that gap is where the next attempt will break.

Take the man whose morning prayer kept dying on late nights. A system that holds for him does not just say "pray at 6 am". It also says when his evening ends, what counts as a miss, and what he does the morning after one.

Work it in writing

  • Write each law in your own words next to one of your goals
  • Match every Step 3 obstacle to the law that answers it
  • Mark any obstacle that no law covers yet
  • Rewrite one goal so it would pass every law

The Weekly Scorecard (Month 1 under Your monthly tools) is these laws put into practice, one week at a time. If you set it up during your first week, look at it again now: you will probably see why each column is there.

Before Step 5: write down the one law you have broken most often, and what you are changing.

lessons.title: Step 5: the four pillars
lessons.html:
Download the Step 5 worksheet (PDF)

A man can hold one area of his life together for a while by letting the others slide. He gets serious at work and disappears at home. He fixes his health and stops praying. The four pillars exist to stop that trade. Each one carries weight, and the structure leans when one is ignored.

Score yourself honestly on each pillar

As you work through the worksheet, place your Step 2 goals under the pillar each one belongs to. Most men find the same thing: their goals pile up under one or two pillars and leave another one empty.

An empty pillar is not a failure. It is information. It is often where the Step 3 obstacles were hiding, because nothing in your plan was protecting it.

Your action from this step

  • Sort every current goal under one of the four pillars
  • Circle the pillar with the fewest goals
  • Add one small, scheduled decision to that pillar for next week
  • Put that decision on your Weekly Scorecard

Your monthly tools are organized to help here. When a pillar is thin, use the tool that speaks to it: the marriage tools, the fatherhood tools, or the faith and discipleship tools.

Before Step 6: tell your accountability partner, or the monthly call, which pillar was empty and the one decision you added.

lessons.title: Step 6: why you need a system
lessons.html:
Download the Step 6 worksheet (PDF)

By now you have a sentence, goals, an honest list of what stopped you, the laws, and the pillars. This step is the reason all of it has to live in a system rather than in your head. Men do not lack conviction. You meant it every time. What was missing was something that keeps working on the days conviction does not show up.

Mood versus mechanism

Picture two men with the same goal: a weekly date night. The first man plans to do it "when things calm down". The second has Friday at 7 written down, a sitter booked on the first of the month, and a rule that a cancelled Friday moves to Saturday, never to "sometime". Three months later, only one of them is still going on dates. Both of them meant it.

The difference is not character. It is that one of them built a mechanism, and the other relied on a mood.

Turn your work so far into one weekly system

  1. Take the goals you sorted under the four pillars in Step 5.
  2. For each, write a time, a miss and a test, the same way the Weekly Scorecard asks.
  3. Decide when your Sunday review happens and put it in your calendar as a repeating event.
  4. Decide who you will tell when you miss. That can be your wife, a friend, or your accountability partner.

Before Step 7: your system should fit on one page and run without you having to remember to be motivated. Send a photo of it to your accountability partner.

lessons.title: Step 7: God at the center
lessons.html:
Download the Step 7 worksheet (PDF)

A system built only on your own strength will eventually run into the limits of your own strength. The last step puts the whole thing in its right order. The goal was never to become a more efficient version of yourself. It was to become the man God is calling you to be, and to let the system serve that.

Read your Step 1 sentence again

Before you open the worksheet, go back to the sentence you wrote in Step 1. Read it slowly and ask where God is in it. For some men He is already there. For others, the sentence describes a good man who is doing it alone.

Work through the worksheet with that sentence beside you. If it needs to change, change it. Everything in your system gets checked against this sentence, so this is the one place it has to be right.

Make it part of the system, not a separate hope

  • Give prayer a time on your Weekly Scorecard, the same as every other decision
  • Start your Sunday review by reading your Step 1 sentence and praying over the week ahead
  • Choose one faith tool from your monthly tools to work through next
  • Name one man you will pray for by name this week

You have finished the framework

You now have a standard, goals, an honest list of obstacles, laws, four pillars, a weekly system, and the right center for it. That is the whole framework. From here, the work is running it every week and using your monthly tools when a pillar needs support.

Bring what changed in your Step 1 sentence, if anything, to the next monthly call.

lessons.title: Month 1: the Weekly Scorecard and Forty Cards
lessons.html:
You finished Step 1 with a sentence that names the man you are building. This month you give that sentence two things it has never had: a daily action and a weekly score. By day 30 you should have four filled-in Scorecards and around twenty-five cards done.

Your next set of tools opens in 30 days. It builds on the Scorecard habit you start now, so the most important thing this month is not to skip a Sunday.

How the two tools work together

Forty Cards gives you one specific action a day. The Weekly Scorecard is where you count how many days you actually did it. The cards supply the action. The Scorecard shows you the truth about it.

Here is how one week can look. Your Step 1 sentence says you are a man who is present at home. On Monday you draw a card: "Ask your wife one question about her day and do not look at your phone until she has finished answering." You do it at 6:15 PM, right after you walk in. On Sunday night your Scorecard shows 5 out of 7 days. That is a number, not a feeling, and next week you try to beat it.

Your setup this week

  • Print the Scorecard, or open the spreadsheet version, and write your Step 1 sentence at the top
  • Pick a fixed time for your daily card, such as the first ten minutes after you get home
  • Choose one person who will see your Scorecard every Sunday
  • Put the deck where you will see it at that time, not in a drawer

Check yourself on day 30

Count your four Scorecards. If every one has a number on it, the habit is working, even when the numbers are low. If a week is blank, you have found your weak spot: write down what happened that Sunday and move your review to a time that still holds on a bad week. A blank page tells you more than a perfect one.

Download both tools below.

lessons.title: Month 2: the Husband's Devotional and Couples Conversation Cards
lessons.html:
Last month you built a weekly score. This month you point it at your marriage. Add one new line to your Scorecard: prayed for her by name. Then add one evening a week for the Couples Cards. By the end of the month you should have 30 mornings of prayer and four conversations on paper.

Mornings: pray for her before the day takes over

The devotional gives you one short reading and one specific prayer for your wife each morning. Keep it specific: "Lord, give her patience with the kids today" is a prayer. "Bless my wife" is a wish. In a randomized study, people who prayed specifically for their partner every day for four weeks were rated as more committed than people who only thought good thoughts about their partner. Four weeks is exactly this month.

Tie it to something you already do every morning, such as before you pick up your phone or while the coffee brews. On your Scorecard, mark each day you prayed.

One evening a week: the conversation cards

Pick a night and a time, for example Thursday at 8:30 PM after the kids are in bed. Phones go in another room. Draw two or three cards and take turns. The cards start light and get more personal, and that order is deliberate: closeness grows when questions go a little deeper each time, not when you start with the hardest one.

Your job is to listen more than you answer. If she says something you want to argue with, ask one more question instead.

Check yourself on day 60

  • At least 20 mornings marked on your Scorecards
  • Four card evenings that actually happened on the night you chose
  • One thing you learned about her that you did not know on day 30
  • If you missed an evening, a new night written down that you can keep

Next month's tool, the Godly Husband Field Guide, builds directly on these habits, so keep both going. Download this month's tools below.

lessons.title: Month 3: the Godly Husband Field Guide
lessons.html:
Month three is where most men quit a new habit. A daily habit takes a median of about 66 days to become automatic, which means you are right at the point where it either sticks or slips. This month gives you something bigger to work on so the habits from months one and two have a reason to keep going.

The Field Guide runs for eight weeks, one section a week. You will finish it partway through month four, and that is fine: the point is the weekly rhythm, not the speed.

Set the rhythm before you open it

Choose one 30-minute slot a week and treat it like an appointment. Sunday evening works for many men because it sits next to the Scorecard review you already do. Read one section, answer its questions in writing, and pick the single action it asks for that week.

Here is how that can look. The section on leading at home asks you to name one recurring decision you have been leaving to your wife by default. You write down "what we do with Saturday mornings." Your action for the week is to bring her a plan for this Saturday by Thursday night, and ask what she would change. On your Scorecard that becomes one line: done or not done.

Use the tracker

The spreadsheet tracker lists each week's action so you can see the whole eight weeks at once. Fill in the action on Sunday and mark it on Saturday. Across 117 studies, structured marriage education measurably improved communication, and longer programs did better than one-off advice. Eight weeks of steady work is the long version.

Check yourself on day 90

  • Four sections done, each with its written answers
  • Four weekly actions marked done or not done, honestly
  • Your morning prayer and weekly card evening still on your Scorecard
  • One change your wife would notice without you pointing it out

lessons.title: Month 4: the Father's Field Guide and Father and Son Cards
lessons.html:
For three months you have built the system around your marriage. This month you extend it to your children. The research here is specific: across 16 long-term studies of more than 22,000 children, what was linked to how kids turned out was a father's direct engagement, not just being in the house. Being home and being engaged are different things, and the Scorecard is about to show you which one you are doing.

If you do not have children at home, use this month for a nephew, a younger man at church, or a son who has grown up. The cards work with any of them.

Start with an honest count

Before you open the Field Guide, add a line to this week's Scorecard: one-on-one time with each child, phone away, at least 15 minutes. Mark it every day. Most men are surprised by the number. That number is your starting point, not a verdict.

Then add two rhythms

Weekly, the Field Guide. Work one section a week in the same slot you used for last month's guide. Each section ends with one decision with a time attached. For example: "Every Tuesday at 6:30 PM, I take my son to the hardware store or the park, just us."

Twice a week, the cards. Use the Father and Son Cards in places where talking is easy and eye contact is optional: the car, a walk, washing dishes side by side. Ask the card's question, then follow up once. If he gives a one-word answer, that is still a conversation, and the next card will go better.

Check yourself on day 120

  • Your one-on-one count is higher than in week one
  • Four Field Guide sections done, each with a dated decision
  • At least six card conversations
  • One thing your child told you this month that you did not already know

lessons.title: Month 5: the Christian Marriage Workbook and the Prayer Strategy
lessons.html:
In month three you worked on how you lead at home. This month you work on time together, and you widen your prayer from your wife to your whole household. The Marriage Workbook is built around one weekly block of time as a couple. In a study of about 1,600 couples, those who spent time together at least once a week were about 3.5 times as likely to describe their marriage as very happy. That is a link, not proof that the time caused it, but it is a link worth acting on.

The workbook: eight sessions, one evening a week

You already have a weekly card evening from month two. Turn it into a workbook evening: same night, same time, phones out of the room. Each session has a short reading, questions for both of you and one thing to try before the next session.

A practical tip: read the session yourself the day before so you are not leading it cold. If a session opens something hard, you do not have to finish it that night. Write down where you stopped and come back to it next week.

The Prayer Strategy: a list, a time and a record

Your morning prayer for your wife has run for three months. The Prayer Strategy gives you a written list of the people in your house, a specific request for each one and a column to record what happened. Keep the morning time you already have and add one name a day from the list. Once a week, at your Scorecard review, read back the record. Seeing answers written down is what keeps the habit honest.

Check yourself on day 150

  • Four workbook evenings done on your chosen night
  • Your prayer list written, with a request for every person in your house
  • At least one answer recorded in the prayer log
  • Your Scorecard still running every Sunday since month one

lessons.title: Month 6: the Men's Bible Study and the Discipleship Workbook
lessons.html:
For five months you have built a system for yourself and your home. This month you take it outside your house. Step 7 put God at the center. The Bible Study and the Discipleship Workbook make that something you practice on a schedule and with other men, not only something you believe.

With this month, you have all eleven tools. From here on, the Club adds one members-only tool each month.

Choose your track

The Men's Bible Study is eight weeks built for a small group. If you can gather two or three other men, even on a video call, use this one. Pick a weekly time, send them the PDF and lead the first session yourself. You do not need to be an expert. Each session has the reading, the questions and the one thing each man commits to before next week.

The Discipleship Workbook is for the weeks you are on your own. It turns faith into written decisions with a time attached, using the same when-and-where planning you have used since Step 1. The tracker shows your eight weeks on one page.

Many men use both: the workbook on their own during the week and the study with other men on the weekend.

Your six-month review

At the end of this month, lay your Scorecards from month one beside this month's. Then answer three questions in writing:

  • Which line on your Scorecard has improved the most since month one
  • Which habit slipped, and what time or trigger would bring it back
  • Could someone in your house tell something changed, without you telling them

If you can answer the last one with a specific example, the system is working. Bring your answer to the next monthly call so other men can hear what six months looks like.

lessons.title: The monthly live call and your accountability partner
lessons.html:
The tools in this Club tell you what to do and when. These two things make sure someone notices whether you did it. Across 138 experiments, tracking progress helped people reach more of their goals, and it worked best when the progress was reported to someone else (Harkin, 2016). Your Weekly Scorecard is the tracking. The call and your partner are the someone else.

The monthly live call

When: the second Tuesday of every month, 7:00 to 8:00 PM Central. The next calls are November 10, December 8, January 12 and February 9.

Where: Google Meet, at meet.google.com/pzg-pjvw-yvu. It's the same link every month. Keep it inside the Club.

What happens: one hour with Brian and the other members. Each man who wants to says, in one sentence, what his Scorecard showed this month: the number of days he kept his system, and the one miss that keeps coming back. Then we work on the misses. Nobody is made to talk, and the call is not recorded.

Before each call

  • Have the last four Weekly Scorecards in front of you
  • Count your kept days as a number, for example 17 out of 28, not "pretty good"
  • Pick the one miss you want help with and write it in one line
  • Join two minutes early from a quiet room

Your accountability partner

Opt in once with the button below. On the first of each month you'll get an email introducing you to one other member. He is your partner for that month.

Every Sunday night, send him a photo of your Scorecard, and he sends you his. Your reply only needs one line: "Got it. What's the plan for the misses?" If he hasn't sent his by Monday morning, ask for it. That question is the whole job.

To stop, reply "stop pairs" to any Club email.

How to know it's working

At the end of each month, compare your kept days with the month before. If the number went up, or the same miss showed up less often, it's working. If it didn't, bring that number to the next call. That's exactly what the call is for.
